name: Discipline and Behavior Data
title: Discipline and Behavior Data
answer: Discipline and behavior data is the practice of using AI features in spreadsheets and student information system reports to break down discipline records by group, school, and type of offense so that unfair patterns become visible. It matters because some groups of students are disciplined more often or more harshly than others for similar behavior, and seeing those patterns tells administrators where to look more closely. The same data can also support positive behavior programs and restorative conversations, but the judgment about what any pattern means stays with people.

sections.body: This idea is about examining discipline records systematically rather than trusting impressions. AI features in spreadsheets and student information system reports can sort discipline data by group, by school, and by type of offense, which surfaces patterns that might otherwise stay hidden. The problem it solves is that unequal discipline can persist unnoticed when nobody looks at the data in a structured way. Once patterns appear, they do not prove wrongdoing on their own, but they show where to look more closely. The point is to direct attention, not to deliver a verdict.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, administrators use AI features in spreadsheets and student information system reports to break discipline data down by group, school, and type of offense, then review the patterns that emerge. Positive behavior intervention and support teams already meet regularly to review data, looking at when and where behavior problems happen, and AI can chart that data and highlight patterns while the team decides what they mean. A spike in problems after lunch, for example, might trace back to hunger, crowding, or a single conflict that a chart cannot reveal. For restorative practices, a teacher or counselor can use AI to draft conversation scripts or questions for a restorative circle, with the adult leading the conversation and adapting to the students involved. Students can also practice handling conflict through role play with a school configured tool, followed by discussion with an adult. The text does not give separate guidance by grade band.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this area as one where fairness in data analysis is harder than it looks. It cites a study of test score predictions finding that balancing the number of students from each group in the data did not guarantee fair predictions (Li et al., 2026). The book applies that same lesson to discipline, noting that a tool which looks balanced can still produce unfair results. The practical conclusion drawn is that people must check outcomes, not just inputs. Beyond that study, the text describes practice rather than presenting further research on discipline data itself.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on what data and AI can decide. A tool that appears balanced can still produce unfair results, so checking outcomes rather than inputs is required. AI can chart discipline data and highlight patterns, but the team decides what the patterns mean, and a chart cannot reveal whether a spike in problems after lunch comes from hunger, crowding, or a single conflict. In restorative work, the adult leads the conversation and adapts to the students involved, and role play with a school configured tool is followed by discussion with an adult. The decisions about meaning, response, and repair stay with people.
